title: Hackers Hit Platform Used by Fox, BBC and Major Banks
excerpt: This week’s cyber chaos has hit some of the world’s biggest companies.
content_html:
TECHNICAL DIFFICULTIES

This week’s cyber chaos has hit some of the world’s biggest companies.

Hackers were able to mine data from 178 sites across several global industries—including media giants CNN and BBC—through a breach of a single platform, cybersecurity experts have revealed.

An unidentified hacker added malicious code to the Optimizely Web Experimentation program, which allows businesses to test and personalize websites, to skim payment cards, swap cryptocurrency wallets, and steal screenshots from an unknown number of consumer devices.

So far, cybersecurity firm Report URI confirmed a little over $7,000 in cryptocurrency exchanges were deposited into the hacker’s account on Tuesday.

Optimizely is used by many organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Zoom, Alaska Airlines, and IKEA. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the hackers added a near-match of Optimizely’s code to the affected organizations’ sites, allowing the attack to go unnoticed.

Researchers are unsure how the hackers gained access to each site and have no way of knowing how many credit cards and other payment methods were skimmed in the last two days.

The malicious code was detected on the BBC’s website on Monday. Since then, hackers have continually modified the code in order to gain access to more sites.

Optimizely did not respond to a request for comment from the Daily Beast, but told ABC that the company “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability.”

The company added in a status update that it was able to remove the vulnerability and fix the code on its customers’ sites. It is unclear whether every site was fully repaired or whether the hackers still have access.

“We’ve fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects,” the company wrote. “We’ve also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered.”

Some of the affected companies issued statements in the wake of the incident.

“Zoom is aware of the Optimizely security incident,” the videoconference company wrote. “As a precautionary measure, Zoom has disabled Optimizely across our production environments. At this time, we have not identified any impact to customer data. We continue to monitor the situation closely.”

“We immediately investigated this issue and ceased our use of Optimizely,” Equifax said in a statement to KPRC 2. “We have not identified evidence of any compromise to our systems or impact to our data.”

After several large-scale tech incidents in the last few days, some have expressed worry that the outages could have come from attacks on U.S. digital infrastructure.

Donald Trump’s national intelligence chief, Jay Clayton, told CNBC on Tuesday that the recent stream of cyberattacks and outages are unrelated and not “a coordinated effort by a nation-state.”

“Many people are patching their systems; they know that their legacy systems have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated, they don’t work well with new systems,” Clayton said. “This is not something that is a coordinated cyber attack or state-sponsored effort against the U.S.”

Editor’s note: We updated the headline to clarify that the breach occurred at Optimizely, a third-party website testing platform used by CNN and other companies.
